reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Descending perineum syndrome is excessive downward descent of the perineum and pelvic floor during straining, reflecting weakness of the pelvic-floor musculature and its supports
It presents with obstructed defecation, a sensation of incomplete evacuation, perineal aching or pain, and, over time, faecal incontinence as pudendal neuropathy develops
Chronic excessive straining is both a cause and a consequence, creating a self-perpetuating cycle of descent, incomplete evacuation, and further straining
The condition is closely linked to repeated stretch injury of the pudendal nerves, which progressively weakens the sphincter and pelvic floor and contributes to incontinence
Clinically the perineum balloons below the plane of the ischial tuberosities on straining, and this can be quantified with a perineometer or on defecating proctography
It frequently coexists with rectocele, rectal intussusception, and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome as part of a spectrum of pelvic-floor dysfunction
Management is predominantly conservative: avoidance of straining, stool bulking and softening, and biofeedback pelvic-floor retraining
Surgery has a limited and carefully selected role, as operations may not reverse established neuropathy and outcomes for isolated perineal descent are unpredictable
reference.pathophysiology: The pelvic floor normally provides dynamic support that limits downward movement of the perineum during defecation. In descending perineum syndrome, weakness of the levator ani and supporting connective tissue, often following childbirth, ageing, and years of excessive straining, allows abnormal downward ballooning of the perineum when intra-abdominal pressure rises. This descent stretches and repeatedly injures the pudendal nerves as they pass around the ischial spines, producing a progressive neuropathy that weakens the external anal sphincter and pelvic floor and predisposes to faecal incontinence. The descent also impairs the normal anorectal angulation and evacuatory mechanics, causing incomplete emptying that provokes further straining, perpetuating both the descent and the nerve injury. Associated mucosal prolapse and intussusception may produce solitary rectal ulcer changes.
additionalDifferentials: Rectal intussusception or full-thickness rectal prolapse
Enterocele or multi-compartment pelvic organ prolapse
additionalInvestigations: Defecating proctography to quantify perineal descent and associated abnormalities
Dynamic pelvic-floor MRI for multi-compartment assessment
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion for evacuatory and sphincter function
Pudendal nerve terminal motor latency or neurophysiological testing where available
Endoanal ultrasound to assess sphincter integrity in incontinent patients
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a mass suggesting neoplasia
A persistent solitary rectal ulcer requiring biopsy to exclude malignancy
Rapidly progressive incontinence or neurological deficit
Symptoms disproportionate to findings, prompting a wider search
reference.prognosis: Descending perineum syndrome tends to be chronic and progressive; conservative measures and biofeedback can relieve symptoms and slow progression, but established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence are difficult to reverse, and surgical results for isolated perineal descent are unpredictable.
pitfalls: Encouraging or overlooking continued straining, which perpetuates descent and nerve injury
Attributing symptoms to a single finding and missing the wider pelvic-floor disorder
Expecting surgery to reverse established pudendal neuropathy and incontinence
Failing to biopsy a coexisting solitary rectal ulcer
Neglecting biofeedback and bowel regulation as first-line therapy
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on pelvic-floor and obstructed defecation disorders
Standard reference texts on pelvic-floor dysfunction and pudendal neuropathy
management: Begin conservative bowel management to break the straining cycle: a high-fibre diet, adequate fluids, stool softeners or laxatives, and modification of defecation technique to avoid straining
Provide pelvic-floor rehabilitation with biofeedback to correct dyssynergic defecation and reduce excessive straining
Manage associated faecal incontinence with stool-firming agents, perineal skin care and consideration of sacral neuromodulation
Treat coexisting pelvic-floor pathology such as rectocele, rectal intussusception and solitary rectal ulcer syndrome as part of the wider dysfunction
Reserve surgery for selected cases and counsel that results for isolated perineal descent are unpredictable
Assess and monitor with defecating proctography, anorectal manometry and pudendal nerve studies within a pelvic-floor multidisciplinary team
